title: Animal Kingdom
tagline: Symmetry, germ layers, coelom and segmentation: the criteria that sort every animal phylum.

overview.intro: The animal kingdom holds more than a million described species, and the classification that makes them manageable rests on a handful of structural criteria rather than on size or habit. This chapter builds those criteria first — levels of organisation, symmetry, germ layers, coelom, segmentation and notochord — and then works through the phyla in ascending complexity, from Porifera and Cnidaria to Chordata, with the practical classes of Chordata at the end. Every examination paper in this area asks the same three things: give the diagnostic features of a phylum, compare two phyla in a table, and identify an animal from a description and place it with reasons.

facts.label: Criteria of classification
facts.value: Levels of organisation, symmetry, germ layers, coelom, segmentation and presence or absence of a notochord.

facts.label: Coelom
facts.value: A body cavity lined by mesoderm: true coelomates, pseudocoelomates with a cavity between mesoderm and endoderm, and acoelomates with none.

facts.label: Notochord
facts.value: A rod of mesodermal cells stiffening the embryonic axis; its presence defines the chordates.

facts.label: Metamerism
facts.value: Serial repetition of body segments, seen in annelids, arthropods and vertebrates as evidence of shared ancestry.

learningOutcomes: State the criteria used in animal classification and apply each one.
List the major phyla with two diagnostic features each and one example.
Compare poriferans, cnidarians, flatworms, roundworms, annelids, arthropods and chordates in tabular form.
Distinguish the three types of body cavity and give an example of each.
Place an unfamiliar animal in a phylum and justify each character used.

blocks.text: Before any phylum can be compared, the criteria that separate them must be stated precisely, because the marks in a classification question are for the criteria, not for the names. Levels of organisation describe how cells are arranged: cellular grade, as in sponges, where cells carry out functions independently; tissue grade, as in cnidarians, where cells of one kind form tissues; organ grade, as in flatworms; and organ-system grade, as in chordates, where several organs work together as systems. Symmetry describes the arrangement of parts around an axis: radial symmetry, in which any plane through the central axis divides the animal into equal halves, suits sedentary or floating animals such as jellyfish and hydra; bilateral symmetry, with a single plane dividing the animal into mirror-image left and right halves, accompanies cephalisation, the concentration of sensory organs and nerve tissue in a head, and suits active directional movement; and asymmetry, in which no plane divides the animal, is found in most sponges. Germ layers count the embryonic tissue layers: diploblastic animals have ectoderm and endoderm only, with a non-cellular mesoglea between, while triploblastic animals also have mesoderm, from which muscles, the circulatory system and the excretory system develop. Coelom asks where the body cavity lies relative to the gut and the mesoderm, and segmentation asks whether the body repeats as a series of metameres. The last criterion, the notochord, is a flexible rod ventral to the nerve cord that supports the embryonic axis, and its presence separates the chordates from every other phylum.

items: Levels of organisation: cellular, tissue, organ and organ-system grade, each more integrated than the last.
Radial symmetry suits sedentary or floating life; bilateral symmetry accompanies a head and directional movement.
Diploblastic animals have two germ layers with a mesoglea between; triploblastic animals have three.
Coelom is a cavity completely lined by mesoderm; its absence or partial lining defines acoelomates and pseudocoelomates.
Metamerism is the repetition of segments, most obvious in annelids and arthropods.
The notochord, a dorsal rod supporting the embryonic axis, defines the chordates.
Cephalisation — a head with sense organs and nerve ganglia — accompanies bilateral symmetry.

items.note: A radial body catches food and danger from every direction at once, which suits an animal drifting with the current rather than chasing prey.
It moves forward in one direction, so sensory organs gather at the front and the body divides into mirror-image halves.

blocks.text: The invertebrate phyla are best learned as a ladder of increasing organisation, each solving a problem the previous one could not. Porifera, the sponges, are cellular grade and asymmetrical or radially symmetrical as adults, with a porous body built around a system of canals, spicules or spongin fibres for support, and collar cells, the choanocytes, that create a water current and trap food particles; they have no true tissues and no nervous system. Cnidaria, the coelenterates, are tissue grade, diploblastic and radially symmetrical, with a gastrovascular cavity opening by a single mouth surrounded by tentacles armed with cnidocytes containing nematocysts — the stinging capsules that paralyse prey — and they alternate between a polyp and a medusa form, as in Hydra, Obelia, Aurelia and the coral polyps. Platyhelminthes, the flatworms, are the first triploblastic animals, with organ grade of organisation, bilateral symmetry and a gastrovascular cavity with only one opening, so food enters and waste leaves through the mouth; the free-living planaria is a predator while Fasciola the liver fluke and Taenia the tapeworm are parasitic, the latter having lost the gut entirely and absorbing food through a syncytial tegument. Nematoda, the roundworms, are pseudocoelomates with a cylindrical unsegmented body, a complete alimentary canal with separate mouth and anus, a tough cuticle for protection and longitudinal muscles only, so they move by thrashing rather than in waves; Ascaris, the large intestinal roundworm, and Enterobius, the pinworm, are the standard examples. Annelida, the segmented worms, are the first true coelomates, with segmentation clearly marked, circular and longitudinal muscles acting against the fluid-filled coelom for peristalsis, a closed blood system in the earthworm with haemoglobin in the plasma, and paired nephridia as excretory organs; the earthworm is the standard example, and the leech and the marine sandworm are its familiar relatives. Arthropoda is the largest phylum of all, with a cuticle of chitin that must be shed as the animal grows, jointed appendages that can be modified into antennae, mouthparts, walking legs, swimmerets or gills, an open circulatory system in which haemolymph bathes the organs, and a well-developed nervous system with a brain and a ventral nerve cord; the classes Crustacea, such as the crab and prawn, Myriapoda, the centipede and millipede, Insecta, the largest class with three body regions and three pairs of legs, and Arachnida, the spider and scorpion with four pairs of legs and no antennae. Mollusca is the second largest phylum, with a soft body, a muscular foot for movement, a mantle that secretes a calcareous shell in most forms, a rasping radula for feeding, and a well-developed coelom reduced to cavities around the organs, with the heart in a haemocoel; the snail and slug are gastropods, the mussel and oyster bivalves, and the squid and octopus cephalopods with a reduced shell, closed circulation and the most developed invertebrate nervous system.

items: Porifera: cellular grade, porous canal system, choanocytes for food and water current, spicules for support, no true tissues.
Cnidaria: diploblastic and radially symmetrical, cnidocytes with nematocysts, gastrovascular cavity with one opening, polyp and medusa forms.
Platyhelminthes: first triploblastic, bilateral, acoelomate, one opening to the gut, free-living planaria and parasitic flukes and tapeworms.
Nematoda: pseudocoelomate, cylindrical unsegmented body, complete alimentary canal, cuticle and longitudinal muscles only.
Annelida: true coelomate and segmented, closed circulation, nephridia, circular and longitudinal muscles for peristalsis.
Arthropoda: largest phylum, chitinous cuticle shed at each moult, jointed appendages, open circulation, insects the largest class.
Mollusca: soft body with foot, mantle and shell, radula, well-developed organ systems; gastropods, bivalves and cephalopods.
Compare phyla on the same criteria every time: organisation, symmetry, germ layers, coelom, segmentation and appendages.

items.text: A sponge is not a plant
items.note: Its choanocytes beat to drive water through the canals and it has no cell walls, which places it in Animalia despite its stationary habit.
Jointed legs, wings and a cuticle that prevents water loss let insects exploit land habitats that exclude most other invertebrates.

learn.title: Phylum Chordata and the vertebrate classes

blocks.text: Chordates are recognised by four characters that appear at some stage of development: a notochord dorsal to the gut, a hollow dorsal nerve cord lying above it, pharyngeal gill slits in the pharyngeal region, and a post-anal tail. The notochord is present in the embryo of all chordates and is replaced by the vertebral column in the vertebrates, the subphylum Vertebrata. The nerve cord is dorsal and hollow, in contrast to the ventral solid nerve cord of annelids and arthropods. The pharyngeal slits function as gill slits in aquatic chordates and are modified into parts of the ear and throat in terrestrial forms. The post-anal tail persists as a vestige in humans and as a powerful swimming organ in fish. Below the vertebrates, Urochordata such as the sea squirt and Cephalochordata such as Branchiostoma, the lancelet, retain the notochord throughout life in at least part of the body. Vertebrates are divided into classes that differ chiefly in respiration, thermoregulation, heart structure and reproduction. Pisces, the fishes, respire through gills, are cold-blooded or poikilothermic, have a two-chambered heart with one atrium and one ventricle, lateral line sense organs and fins for swimming, with a large air-bladder or swim bladder giving buoyancy. Amphibia, the amphibians, have a three-chambered heart with two atria and one ventricle, moist glandular skin through which exchange also occurs, larvae with gills that metamorphose into lung-bearing adults, and eggs without shells laid in water, as in the frog, the toad and the limbless caecilian. Reptilia are the first fully terrestrial vertebrates: dry skin with keratinised scales or scutes that prevent water loss, lungs for respiration throughout life, a three-chambered heart in which the ventricle is incompletely divided, cold-bloodedness, and amniotic eggs with a shell laid on land, as in the lizard, the snake, the turtle and the crocodile. Aves, the birds, are warm-blooded or homoeothermic, have feathers and forelimbs modified into wings, pneumatic hollow bones that reduce weight, a four-chambered heart for efficient oxygen delivery, air sacs connected to the lungs for a continuous flow of air during both inhalation and exhalation, and hard-shelled eggs. Mammalia are warm-blooded, have skin with sweat and sebaceous glands and hair for insulation, a four-chambered heart, lungs for respiration, and most importantly mammary glands that secrete milk for the young, together with a diaphragm for ventilation and a placenta in the eutherians. The comparison of heart chambers and of thermoregulation across these classes is a standard examination table, and it tracks the evolutionary trend towards endothermy, efficient circulation and independence from water for reproduction.

items: Four chordate characters: notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal slits and post-anal tail.
In vertebrates the notochord is replaced by the vertebral column.
Urochordates and cephalochordates retain the notochord; vertebrates replace it with vertebrae.
Pisces: gills, poikilothermic, two-chambered heart, fins and a swim bladder.
Amphibia: three-chambered heart, moist skin, gilled larvae, shell-less eggs laid in water.
Reptilia: dry scaly skin, lungs, incompletely divided ventricle, amniotic shelled egg laid on land.
Aves: feathers, wings, pneumatic bones, four-chambered heart, air sacs, warm-blooded.
Mammalia: hair, mammary glands, four-chambered heart, diaphragm, mostly placental young.
The trend across classes is towards a divided heart, endothermy and reproduction freed from water.

items.text: A frog changes how it breathes
items.note: The tadpole breathes with gills, and after metamorphosis the adult uses lungs and its moist skin, which is why a frog must stay damp.
Pneumatic bones reduce weight for flight, and the air sacs that enter them also supply the lungs with fresh air on both the in and the out breath.

items.meaning: A flexible rod of mesodermal cells supporting the embryonic axis, replaced by vertebrae in vertebrates.
The serial repetition of body segments with similar structures.
Maintaining a constant body temperature by internal means, as birds and mammals do.
A shelled egg with extra-embryonic membranes that lets reproduction occur on land.

learn.title: Classification in practice: the method for identification questions

blocks.text: Identification questions are answered by running the animal through the criteria in the order in which they divide the kingdom most sharply. Ask first whether there is a backbone: no places the animal among the invertebrate phyla, yes takes it to the vertebrate classes. Among invertebrates, ask whether the body has joints and a chitinous exoskeleton, which gives Arthropoda at once, then whether the body is segmented with a true coelom, which gives Annelida, then whether the body is a flattened or cylindrical worm with no coelom or a pseudocoelom, which separates Platyhelminthes from Nematoda, then whether there is a shell and a muscular foot, which gives Mollusca, and whether there are stinging cells, which gives Cnidaria, with sponges remaining as the only animals without true tissues. Among vertebrates, ask how the animal breathes and whether the skin is moist or dry, then how many heart chambers are present, and finally whether it has feathers, hair or scales. The habit that converts the placement into full marks is quoting each character as evidence in a line: writing Arthropoda earns little, while writing Arthropoda because the body is segmented, the exoskeleton is of chitin, the appendages are jointed and the circulation is open earns everything. Two traps are worth knowing: a crab is not a mollusc despite its shell, because its jointed legs and chitinous exoskeleton make it an arthropod, and a snake is not a fish or a worm because it has lungs, scales and a vertebral column.

items: Ask first whether a backbone is present; it divides the kingdom into vertebrates and invertebrates.
Invertebrate order: joints and exoskeleton, segmentation, body form and coelom, shell, stinging cells, no tissues at all.
Vertebrate order: breathing method, skin covering, heart chambers, then integument such as feathers or hair.
Quote every diagnostic character with the phylum name — the reasoning carries the marks.
Do not classify by habit or size alone: a crab with a shell is an arthropod, not a mollusc.
Give the subphylum or class as well as the phylum whenever the question allows it.

items.note: A cylindrical unsegmented body with a pseudocoelom and a cuticle identifies a roundworm of phylum Nematoda.

keyPoints: Animal classification uses levels of organisation, symmetry, germ layers, coelom, segmentation and the notochord.
Radial symmetry suits a sedentary or floating habit; bilateral symmetry accompanies cephalisation and active movement.
Diploblastic animals have two germ layers; triploblastic animals have three.
A coelom is a cavity completely lined by mesoderm; pseudocoelomates and acoelomates lack this lining.
Sponges are the only animals at cellular grade without true tissues.
Cnidarians have cnidocytes, radial symmetry and a single opening to the gut.
Arthropoda is the largest phylum, characterised by jointed appendages and a chitinous exoskeleton.
Annelids are segmented coelomates with closed circulation and nephridia.
Molluscs have a soft body with a muscular foot, a mantle and usually a shell.
Chordates have a notochord, a dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal slits and a post-anal tail.
Heart chambers increase from two in fish to four in birds and mammals, with thermoregulation becoming homoeothermic.
Mammals are distinguished by mammary glands, hair and a diaphragm.
examFocus: Phylum questions want two diagnostic features and one example — nothing shorter earns full marks.
Comparison tables must use the same criteria as rows for every phylum named.
Identification answers quote each character in a line before stating the phylum.
The vertebrate class table expects heart chambers, thermoregulation, skin, respiration and egg together.

vocabulary.meaning: A body cavity completely lined by mesoderm.
A body cavity not fully lined by mesoderm, as in roundworms.
A stinging cell of cnidarians containing a nematocyst.
Segmentation of the body into a series of similar units.
The flexible supporting rod defining the chordates.
Concentration of sense organs and nervous tissue at the anterior end.
A shelled egg that permits reproduction away from water.
Maintenance of a constant internal body temperature.

questions.prompt: The largest phylum in the animal kingdom is:
questions.explanation: Arthropoda contains more described species than any other phylum, largely through the success of insects.

questions.prompt: Nematodes differ from annelids in having:
questions.explanation: Roundworms are pseudocoelomates, whereas annelids are true coelomates with a closed blood system.

questions.prompt: Nematocysts are found in which phylum?
questions.explanation: Nematocysts are the stinging organelles held within the cnidocytes of cnidarians.

questions.prompt: Which class of vertebrates has a four-chambered heart and pneumatic bones?
questions.explanation: Birds have a complete separation of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood and hollow bones that reduce weight.

questions.prompt: A body cavity that is completely lined by mesoderm is called the __________.
questions.explanation: The presence of a true coelom distinguishes coelomates from acoelomates and pseudocoelomates.

questions.prompt: The stiffening rod found in the embryos of all chordates, and replaced by vertebrae in vertebrates, is the __________.
questions.explanation: It runs dorsal to the gut and defines the phylum Chordata.

questions.prompt: Give two distinguishing features of phylum Arthropoda and name its four classes.
questions.answer: Arthropods have jointed appendages, which permit walking, swimming, feeding and sensory functions, and a tough exoskeleton of chitin that is shed at each moult as the animal grows. They also have an open circulatory system in which haemolymph bathes the organs directly. The four classes are Crustacea such as the crab and prawn, Myriapoda including the centipede and millipede, Insecta containing the three-region body with three pairs of legs, and Arachnida containing spiders and scorpions with four pairs of legs and no antennae.
questions.explanation: Jointed appendages and chitinous exoskeleton, plus the four classes with an example each.

questions.prompt: Why is radial symmetry suited to the life of a jellyfish?
questions.answer: A jellyfish drifts in the water and encounters food, danger and obstacles equally from all directions, so there is no advantage to having a distinct head and back. Radial symmetry arranges the tentacles and sensory structures around a central axis so that the animal can respond and capture prey from any direction. The body is also suited to floating, since the bell-shaped form distributes water pressure evenly around the animal.
questions.explanation: The drifting habit, equal encounter from all directions, and tentacles arranged around the central axis.

questions.prompt: State the four characters of phylum Chordata.
questions.answer: The four characters are a notochord, a flexible rod of mesodermal cells supporting the embryonic axis; a hollow dorsal nerve cord lying above the notochord; pharyngeal gill slits in the pharyngeal region, which function in respiration in aquatic forms; and a post-anal tail, which persists behind the anus in the embryo and in many adults. At least one of these must be present at some stage of development for the animal to be a chordate.
questions.explanation: Notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal slits and post-anal tail, each with a line of explanation.

questions.prompt: Compare phylum Annelida with phylum Arthropoda under the headings of segmentation, exoskeleton, circulation and coelom.
questions.answer: Segmentation appears in both phyla but differs in its extent. In annelids such as the earthworm the segmentation is both external and internal, with the coelom divided by septa and each segment carrying nephridia, so the units are largely similar and serially repeated. In arthropods segmentation is mainly external and the segments are grouped into three functional regions, head, thorax and abdomen, with considerable modification of appendages between segments. The covering also differs: annelids have a thin moist cuticle through which much exchange occurs and no hard skeleton, whereas arthropods possess a rigid exoskeleton of chitin that supports and protects the body and prevents water loss, at the cost of requiring moulting for growth. Circulation separates them sharply, since annelids have a closed circulation with blood confined to vessels and haemoglobin carried in the plasma, while arthropods have an open circulation in which the heart pumps haemolymph through short vessels into sinuses that bathe the organs directly. Both are coelomates, but in annelids the coelom is large, well developed and divided by septa to form a hydrostatic skeleton for burrowing, whereas in arthropods the coelom is reduced and largely taken over by the haemocoel through which the haemolymph circulates.
questions.explanation: All four headings covered for both phyla with a closing comparison of what each difference achieves.

questions.prompt: An animal is found on a rock in a stream. It has a soft body, a broad flat muscular foot, a spiral calcareous shell, a rasping tongue-like structure for feeding and a mantle lining the shell. Identify its phylum and justify each feature.
questions.answer: The soft unsegmented body with a broad muscular foot for locomotion identifies the animal as a mollusc, since the foot is the characteristic locomotory organ of the phylum and is used for crawling or burrowing. The calcareous shell formed by the mantle confirms the placement: the mantle is the dorsal fold of body wall that secretes the shell in all but a few molluscs, and it encloses the pallial cavity in which the gills lie. The rasping tongue-like structure is the radula, a ribbon of chitinous teeth unique to molluscs, used to scrape food from surfaces — absent from bivalves but well developed in grazing gastropods. The spiral form of the shell with a single valve indicates a gastropod such as a snail rather than a bivalve. No jointed appendages are present to suggest an arthropod, and the combination of foot, mantle and radula leaves no other phylum possible: it is a gastropod mollusc.
questions.explanation: Foot, mantle-secreted shell, radula and body form each identified and linked to Mollusca, with the class given.

questions.prompt: Explain how the structure of the frog shows the transition from an aquatic to a terrestrial way of life.
questions.answer: The frog is an amphibian and shows adaptations of both habitats in its structure. As an aquatic breeder it lays shell-less eggs in water, and its larvae, the tadpoles, breathe with gills and swim with a tail — features of a fish-like existence. As an adult it breathes with lungs, but the lungs are simple sac-like structures with little surface area, so the moist glandular skin performs a large share of gas exchange; this is why the skin must stay wet and why frogs are found near water. The three-chambered heart, with two atria and one ventricle, sends some blood to the skin as well as to the lungs, and the incomplete separation of the ventricle mixes some oxygenated and deoxygenated blood — adequate for an animal that is cold-blooded and does not need a high constant metabolic rate. Limbs replace fins, with powerful hind limbs for jumping and webbed feet for swimming, and the absence of a tail in the adult reflects the loss of the larval swimming organ. Together these features show an animal adapted to move and breathe on land while still tied to water for reproduction and for keeping its skin functional.
questions.explanation: The aquatic features, the terrestrial features and the compromises between them, each linked to a structure.
